displayQuote: If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog

meta.title: Who really said "If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Truman. His own presidential library has never confirmed it — the line traces to a 1975 play, and the joke to a 1911 newspaper classified ad.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog'?
meta.ogDescription: Harry Truman never said it. A 1975 one-man play put it in his mouth; the older saying ran as 'IF YOU WANT A FRIEND / Buy a dog' in an 1911 Philadelphia classified ad, and the 'in Washington' form isn't documented before 1985.

answer.label: Not Harry S. Truman — an old advertising saw, put in his mouth by a 1975 play
answer.authorDates: 1918–1991 · American playwright who wrote the fictional Truman line
answer.sourceLine: Truman almost certainly never said this. The first known link between Truman and the saying is a line Samuel Gallu wrote for a fictional Truman in his one-man show Give ’em Hell, Harry! (Viking Press, 1975), p. 8 — and even there the wording is “You want a friend in life, get a dog!”, not “in Washington.” The underlying joke is older still and anonymous: it ran as a Philadelphia Inquirer classified ad in 1911 ↗.

source.heading: The nearest thing to a source

docMeta.dd: Harry S. Truman — no source in his own words has ever been located
Samuel Gallu; New York: Viking Press, 1975, p. 8
“IF YOU WANT A FRIEND / Buy a dog.” — Philadelphia Inquirer classified ad, 19 November 1911, p. 2

source.excerpt: Banks, boy, there’s a bunch of crooks for you. They’re happy to lend you money when you prove you don’t need it. You want a friend in life, get a dog!
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes it is “very unlikely that it was said by Harry Truman,” and identifies Samuel Gallu’s 1975 Give ’em Hell Harry (Viking Press, p. 8) as containing “the first known connection between Truman and the saying” — there rendered “You want a friend in life, get a dog!”

Barry Popik ↗ documents the saying “cited in print since at least 1911,” beginning with a Philadelphia Inquirer classified ad reading “IF YOU WANT A FRIEND / Buy a dog,” and dates the “Washington” form to at least 1985. He also reproduces Ralph Keyes’s verdict in The Quote Verifier (2006), p. 47: “An old saw put in Harry Truman’s mouth.”

The Harry S. Truman Library has never been able to confirm it. Supervisory archivist Sam Rushay told PolitiFact ↗ so directly, and archivist Randy Sowell had already told TeleRead ↗ in 2008 that the play “isn’t footnoted, so we have no idea where he got this saying,” adding: “The truth is that the Trumans were not dog owners.”

English Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Misattributed section, noting it was quoted as Truman’s by both George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton, and that “prior to Gallu’s play there is no actual indication Truman ever said this.”
source.excerptNote: This is Gallu’s stage Truman, not the historical one — and note the wording: “in life,” not “in Washington.” The Washington form is a later drift, dated by Barry Popik to at least 1985.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the popular wording, because no author or first publication has ever been identified for it. The oldest documented ancestor — an anonymous 1911 newspaper classified advertisement — would long since be in the public domain, but it is not this sentence. The nearest documented relative that does have an author, Samuel Gallu’s “You want a friend in life, get a dog!” from Give ’em Hell, Harry! (Viking Press, 1975), is a different line and remains in copyright.

author.name: Samuel Gallu
author.heading: About Samuel Gallu
author.bio: Samuel Gallu wrote and produced across film, theatre and television, but he is remembered above all for Give ’em Hell, Harry!, the one-man Truman show that James Whitmore carried to the screen in 1975. Gallu’s script was not footnoted, so nobody — the Truman Library included — knows where he found the dog line he handed his stage president. He is not the author of the saying, only the first documented person to attach it to Truman; the joke itself was circulating in American newspapers and kennel signage decades before he wrote it down.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a joke climbing the ladder of fame: an anonymous advertising slogan becomes a comedian’s wisecrack, becomes a playwright’s line for a fictional president, and finally becomes the real president’s own words — quoted back at Washington by senators, presidents and candidates.

items.why: Sam Rushay, supervisory archivist at the Harry S. Truman Library and Museum, told PolitiFact: “We have never been able to confirm or verify that President Truman ever wrote or said, ‘If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog.’” PolitiFact rated the attribution False ↗. The Trumans were not dog owners — a cocker spaniel puppy given to them at the White House was passed on to the president’s doctor, and Ralph Keyes records in The Quote Verifier (2006), p. 47 that Harry and Bess “gave away the two that were given to them while they lived in the White House.”

items.scope: “You want a friend in life, get a dog!”
items.why: Ralph Keyes traced the attribution to Gallu’s 1975 one-man show, and Quote Investigator confirms it as the first known connection between Truman and the saying ↗. Truman Library archivist Randy Sowell noted the play is not footnoted, so where Gallu got the line is unknown — and it was published in 1975, three years after Truman died.

items.scope: “If you need a friend, get a dog”
items.why: A Wall Street branch of the same joke. Time reported in 2008 that the “buy a dog” line is most often credited to corporate raider Carl Icahn in the mid-1980s; the version audiences actually remember is Michael Douglas’s Gekko in Wall Street (1987) — “And if you need a friend, get a dog” — written by Stanley Weiser and Oliver Stone, both documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

items.scope: “nobody need want a friend who can get a dog”
items.why: Quote Investigator closes its article with an 1841 citation from Catherine Sinclair’s Modern Flirtations that credits the sentiment to Byron, while explicitly cautioning that “the attribution may be questionable” ↗. Treat it as an early sighting of the idea, not a source.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody owns this sentence. It is an anonymous American advertising saw, in print by 1911, that a 1975 play attached to a president who had already been dead for three years — and no researcher, including Barry Popik ↗ or the Truman Library itself, has ever found Truman saying it.

context.heading: The president who gave the dog away
lead: The line lands because it sounds like Truman — blunt, funny, faintly bitter about the town that chewed him up. The trouble is that Truman was, by every account his own library can find, not a dog person. A cocker spaniel puppy named Feller arrived at the White House as a gift and was quietly rehomed with the president’s physician; a 1948 syndicated column noticed and needled him for it, reporting that Truman admitted “under pressure” that the pup was living elsewhere, and adding that this was “bound to cost Harry more votes.” A reader put the obvious question to columnist E. V. Durling the following year and got the domestic answer: Mrs. Truman thought dogs were too much trouble to care for. Both clippings are reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗.

So the aphorism arrived backwards: not from a lonely president reaching for his dog, but from a playwright writing a president who never had one. Once Gallu’s stage Truman said it, the sentence drifted — “in this life” in a 1975 Los Angeles Times review, “in this world” in a 1978 nursing textbook, and finally “in Washington” by the mid-1980s, at which point it became too useful to politicians to ever go away. Senator Nancy Kassebaum handed it to Alan Greenspan as Truman’s own words in a 1987 New York Times letter; George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton both repeated it as Truman’s, per Wikiquote ↗; John Kasich was still quoting it on the 2016 campaign trail.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording drifted, decade by decade
detailsBody: 1911 — A Philadelphia Inquirer classified ad (19 Nov, p. 2, col. 6) reads simply: “IF YOU WANT A FRIEND / Buy a dog.” Barry Popik traces further printings through 1919, 1924, 1925 and a 1937 Hartford Courant piece prompted by a sales-kennel sign.

1941 — The Hollywood version: comedian Frank Fay’s advice to the newly arrived French director René Clair — “If you’re going to stay in this town and want a friend, go out and buy yourself a dog” — printed in the Dunkirk Evening Observer. Popik notes the “Hollywood” version never caught on.

1975 — Gallu’s stage Truman: “You want a friend in life, get a dog!” A Los Angeles Times stage review the same year already renders it “If you want a friend in this life, get a dog” and treats it as characterisation of the real man.

1978–1987 — A nursing textbook attributes “If you want a friend in this world, get a dog” directly to Truman. Popik dates the “Washington” form to at least 1985; by June 1987 Senator Kassebaum is quoting “If you want a friend in Washington, buy a dog” as Truman’s in the New York Times.
context.pull: “The truth is that the Trumans were not dog owners.” — Randy Sowell, Truman Library archivist

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator states it is "very unlikely that it was said by Harry Truman," identifies Samuel Gallu's 1975 Give 'em Hell Harry (Viking Press, p. 8) as "the first known connection between Truman and the saying" with the wording "You want a friend in life, get a dog!", and reproduces the 1948 Mexia Weekly Herald Feller clipping, the 1949 E. V. Durling column on Mrs. Truman, the 1975 LA Times review ("If you want a friend in this life, get a dog"), the 1978 nursing-book attribution ("in this world"), Kassebaum's 7 June 1987 NYT letter ("buy a dog"), the 1941 Frank Fay / Rene Clair cite, the 2008 Time note on Carl Icahn, Gordon Gekko's line in Wall Street (1987), and an 1841 Catherine Sinclair citation crediting Byron whose "attribution may be questionable." It also credits Ralph Keyes's The Quote Verifier for tracing the attribution to the 1975 play.

Barry Popik's page states the saying has "been cited in print since at least 1911," prints the 19 November 1911 Philadelphia Inquirer classified ad (p. 2, col. 6) "IF YOU WANT A FRIEND / Buy a dog," states "The 'Washington' version is cited from at least 1985," prints the 1941 Frank Fay cite, the 1975 Gallu text at p. 8, the 1985 South Florida Sun-Sentinel and 1987 Kassebaum instances, gives Truman's dates as (1884-1972), and reproduces The Quote Verifier p. 47 including "Harry and his wife, Bess, had no particular fondness for dogs, and gave away the two that were given to them while they lived in the White House" and "Verdict: An old saw put in Harry Truman's mouth."

English Wikiquote lists "If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog" under its Misattributed section, notes it was quoted as Truman's by both George H. W. Bush and Bill Clinton, states it "apparently originates from a line in the portrayal of Truman in the play Give 'Em Hell, Harry (1975) by Samuel Gallu: 'You want a friend in life, get a dog!'", and says "prior to Gallu's play there is no actual indication Truman ever said this."

PolitiFact rated the attribution False and quotes Sam Rushay, supervisory archivist at the Harry S. Truman Library and Museum: "We have never been able to confirm or verify that President Truman ever wrote or said, 'If you want a friend in Washington, get a dog.'" It also notes the misattribution likely stems from Gallu's 1975 play and that Truman gave away the cocker spaniel Feller.

TeleRead (David Rothman) quotes Harry S. Truman Library archivist Randy Sowell: "We've traced this quote back to Samuel Gallu's one-man play, Give 'Em Hell, Harry, in which the Truman character says, 'You want a friend in life, get a dog!'", that the play "isn't footnoted, so we have no idea where he got this saying," and "The truth is that the Trumans were not dog owners... in our extensive research over the years we haven't been able to find that Truman actually said it."
Wikipedia describes Give 'em Hell, Harry! as a 1975 one-man show about Harry S. Truman, written by Samuel Gallu and starring James Whitmore.
Wikipedia gives Samuel Gallu's dates as March 21, 1918 to March 27, 1991, and describes him as an American writer, producer and director working across film, theatre and television.
